The St. Lawrence River. Flowing approximately seven hundred fifty miles from Lake Ontario to the Gulf of St. Lawrence in eastern Canada, the St. Lawrence serves as a crucial shipping corridor linking the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean. Shared between Canada and the United States, it forms a central artery for commerce and hydropower in eastern North America. The river originates at the outflow of Lake Ontario near Kingston, drawing water from all five Great Lakes. Early French explorers named it after Saint Laurent in honor of the Christian martyr Saint Lawrence. Descending about two hundred eighty feet from Lake Ontario to sea level, the river features Niagara Falls as its most dramatic drop, shared with the shorter Niagara River to the west. In the nineteen fifties the Saint Lawrence Seaway was built, a system of locks that allows ocean-going ships to travel deep into North America. The river forms the boundary between Canada and the United States for much of its course, with several islands including the Thousand Islands and multiple hydroelectric dams throughout its length. It was historically crucial for fur trading and early European settlement in North America. In winter the river freezes, requiring icebreakers to maintain year-round navigation and commerce.
